extracted.intended_audience: members of the Royal Society / learned natural philosophers and experimentalists
extracted.subtask_description: Explaining and experimentally reproducing atmospheric optical phenomena (parhelia, halos, mock-suns) via particle shape/orientation hypotheses and lab analogues; includes related practical reports (teaching deaf person, vinegar making, salt-mining).

rubrics_metrics.name: Parhelia/halo causes: oriented cylinders vs round grains
rubrics_metrics.description: That parhelia, halos, arches, and related phenomena are caused by ice particles of differing shapes and orientations — notably 'perpendicular cylinders', 'cylinders parallel to the horizon', and 'round grains'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perpendicular cylinders (axes perpendicular to horizon) produce parhelia by transmitting rays through rounded ends; these can appear coloured like a rainbow or faintly white. Horizontal (couchant) cylinders (axes parallel to the horizon) produce arches that touch halos and can produce parhelia brighter at superior and inferior parts; when particles are round grains, parhelia appear equally strong everywhere. The figure/shape of arches depends on sun altitude and halo diameters; arches touching halos are more strongly enlightened and coloured, indicating parhelia there.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arches, crosses, and other halo features from cylinder orientations
rubrics_metrics.description: Different postures of cylindric particles (perpendicular, horizontal, inclined, or tumbling) account for arches that touch halos, the white cross with paraselenes, and various rods or extraordinary arches near the sun.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Horizontal cylinders produce arches and the horizontal fillet of the white cross (the perpendicular fillet comes from perpendicular cylinders). Inclined cylinders (about half a right angle to horizon) with opaque kernels can generate mock suns, anthelia from intersection of arches, and other rods/arches. Many cylinders in varied postures, moving in the air, can produce vivid halos — each cylinder sends many more rays to the eye than round grains, explaining different brightness/appearance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental reproduction: glass cylinder analogue
rubrics_metrics.description: Reproduce halo/parhelia effects experimentally by using a glass cylinder (about a foot long) with an opaque central kernel, ambient space filled with water, and exposing it to the sun while observing from proper positions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Huygens produced such a glass cylinder (wooden kernel, water instead of transparent ice) and, with the eye placed in proper places, successively observed the reflections and refractions described; from this it is concluded that many similarly shaped small cylinders in the air, in the postures supposed, will reproduce the parhelia and halo appearances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unexplained mock-suns opposite the true sun (limitation / negative finding)
rubrics_metrics.description: Observed mock suns sometimes show directly opposite the true sun; this effect could not be accounted for by round grains or the described cylinders, so its cause must be sought elsewhere if future observations confirm it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors note inability to find, in the round grains or cylinders considered, a mechanism that necessarily produces mock suns meeting in the great white circle parallel to the horizon; treat such occurrences as unresolved and requiring alternative hypotheses or further exact observations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teaching a deaf person: two essential, distinct tasks
rubrics_metrics.description: Teaching a deaf person to speak and to understand a language consists of two very different parts: (1) teaching pronunciation (to utter sounds), and (2) teaching understanding (to know the signification of words), each of which increases the difficulty of the other if neglected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To teach pronunciation, one must show by significant signs the posture and motion of tongue, lips, palate, and other speech organs, confirm correct attempts, indicate differences when incorrect, and use frequent repetition until sounds are fixed. For understanding, one may use written characters or agreed signs to represent conceptions directly (analogous to Chinese characters, numerals, algebraic symbols), so the deaf can learn meanings without relying on sound; with time and practice a deaf person may understand and write as well as hearing people. Start with the most useful language (English in this account), allow extended practice time, and expect gradual but real progress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feasibility and method of teaching language without hearing (use of characters)
rubrics_metrics.description: Letters or characters can be applied to represent conceptions immediately, independent of sounds; this makes it feasible for deaf learners to attain knowledge of language and to communicate via writing or agreed characters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include Chinese characters, numeral figures, and algebraic symbols: where characters express notions independent of their vocalization. Two or more persons can agree on characters to express sense in writing without attending to sound. Therefore, teaching a deaf person via characters (or new/invented agreed signs) is feasible and can lead to real understanding equivalent in content to that of hearing persons, given sufficient time and exercise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Benchmarks for progress in teaching deaf students (empirical timeline)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reported empirical progress milestones from the instructional case: partial speech and comprehension after months; substantial literacy after a year.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the reported case: after somewhat more than two months the student could speak many words (though accuracy and expedition required longer practice). Within a year (the whole stay with the teacher) he had read a great part of the English Bible, expressed himself intelligibly in ordinary affairs, understood letters written to him and wrote answers (not elegantly but intelligibly), and pronounced difficult words in various languages when prompted. These benchmarks indicate realistic expectations for time and improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: French vinegar-making method (practical procedure & quality controls)
rubrics_metrics.description: A two-cask system using a trevet and 'rape' (dried vine twigs/stalks) to sour wine into vinegar by alternate transfer, temperature control, and regular removal of scum and grease.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedure: place a trevet one foot high in each large cask, lay vine twigs and a substance called rape (dried grape stalks) up to within half a foot of the top. Fill one cask with wine, the other half full; each day draw half the wine from the full vessel to fill the half-full one, alternating daily. The half-filled cask heats (indicator of activity); in summer the process takes ~15 days, slower in winter. Full vessel is open at top; half-filled vessel has a wooden cover. Remove scum daily when pouring and scrape grease from cask sides and rape; cleanse rape about yearly to avoid whitish spoiled liquor. In very hot weather draw twice daily. New casks make vinegar more slowly; best wine yields best vinegar, though turned wine also works.

rubrics_metrics.name: Salt-mines extraction and maintenance practices (operational procedures)
rubrics_metrics.description: Descriptions of mine layout, extraction, transport, and structural support practices observed at the Sal-Gem mines near Cracovia (Wieliczka).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mines have multiple descents and ladders reaching great depths, with many interconnected holes dug wherever salt veins continue. Large holes and passages are carefully filled out and supported with strong, well-compacted timber to secure town and works above. Salt is cut in large pieces and later ground; mined salt types (coarse black, finer white, very white crystal) have different values. Horses are kept below to carry salt to the rope-hoist; prolonged underground exposure leads to blindness in horses. Salt springs beneath the mines supply brine for boiling. These operational details imply safety and production standards: robust timbering, staging of extraction, and management of brine processing.
